channel.title: Nicotine Science and Policy
channel.description: Daily digest of views, debates and discussions on nicotine science, policy, regulation and advocacy.

item.title: Plain Packaging and “Drab” Colors: The UK’s Latest Anti-Vape Plan
item.description: Plain packaging for vapes may make products look less appealing, but that is not the same as making policy more effective. For adults trying to move away from cigarettes, product information, differentiation and trust all matter. If lower-risk alternatives are stripped of identity while cigarettes remain familiar and available, regulation may weaken the very appeal that helps switching. Public health should be careful not to make safer options harder to recognise, understand or choose. (Published on July 29, 2026byfiltermag.org)

item.title: Estonia’s proposed nicotine pouch cap will trap more smokers with deadly cigarettes
item.description: A nicotine cap sounds technical, but its consequences could be very real. If Estonia makes pouches too weak to work for adult smokers, the policy may protect cigarettes more than people. Regulation should control quality, access and marketing without removing the features that make smoke-free products viable alternatives. Harm reduction fails when safer options are allowed in name, but made ineffective in practice. (Published on July 29, 2026bysmokefreesweden.org)

item.title: What's Really Inside Nicotine Pouches? | #GFN26ScienceLab
item.description: What is actually inside a nicotine pouch matters more than the assumptions around it. Ingredients, formulation and exposure need to be examined transparently, especially as pouches become part of the wider harm reduction debate. Scrutiny is necessary, but it should be specific: what is in the product, how it is used, and how its risks compare with combustible tobacco. Good regulation starts with chemistry and evidence, not suspicion by category. (Published on July 30, 2026bygfn.tv)

item.title: Does Vaping Impair Skin Healing?
item.description: The skin-healing question sits in a wider clinical grey area: what should patients be told when the evidence is still developing? Vaping should not be presented as harmless, but neither should it be discussed as though it carries the same exposure profile as smoking. For wound recovery, surgery and tissue repair, the useful message is precision: identify possible risks, explain uncertainty, and keep combustion in a separate risk category. Clinical advice is strongest when it helps people understand degrees of harm, not just avoid nuance. (Published on July 30, 2026bydaily-pouch.com)
